en: The Method for Penetrating the Barrier of Prajñā: A wondrous chain of links, inconceivable. The Tathāgata’s profound wisdom encompasses all without exception;
Like snow and moon, he bestows skillful wisdom. For a thousand years, we look up to his fragrant model.
Xuedou’s fourth-generation descendant, Master Shouyi of Benjue, Who once established a society for sutra study.
Through the great power of the vow for universal dissemination, there are those such as Chengzhang who, while living at home, diligently uphold [the teachings].
How admirable is the Master of the Bamboo Grove! He joyfully recites with tireless zeal. Year after year he convenes superior assemblies;
his kindness is represented by the provision of funds. May he hope to deliver immeasurable multitudes, so that they may together realize the state of Perfect Enlightenment.
On a day in the fifth month of the Renchen year of the Zhengde era, Eosan Wetaem respectfully inscribed this preface to the *Dabanruo jing tongguan fa*.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* consists of six hundred fascicles; it was translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Tang dynasty.
Translation: The volumes are numerous and scattered, as vast as a sea of mist; it is not easy for a student to master them.
The Great Master Dayin of Fengcheng Xueyue, employing his skillful wisdom, first devised a method for penetrating the entire work.
Later, the Vinaya Master Yanzhong of Siming attained realization and re-edited it, making it even more refined and rigorous. This method consists of twelve diagrams, utilizing thirteen [categories].
The Dharma consists of twenty-nine realms and eighty-four categories, which serve as its totality.

Generally, among those items listed in the diagrams, some are arranged in rows, some are arranged individually, some occupy single positions, some avoid adjacent positions, some are interspersed, some employ additive methods, and some are linked like hooks and chains.

Whether expanded or abbreviated, it does not exceed one thousand words, yet it completely encompasses the first division, the "Chapter on Difficult-to-Believe and Difficult-to-Understand" (Nanxinjie-pin), totaling one hundred and three fascicles, without a single character being in conflict [with the original].
Alas, how extraordinary this is! Previously, in the region east of the River Zhe, those who had seen it were very few.

It was during the Chunxi era of the Song dynasty that a remarkable monk, carrying the scripture, traveled to Yongdong; he recited it from memory without ceasing, and the prominent local family, the Wo family, [received it].
Chang was filled with doubt. He extracted one or two scrolls to test him;

the recitation was exactly as it had been for the first scroll, and furthermore, the *Guānfǎ* (Method of the Pass) was produced and bestowed upon Cheng-chang. Cheng-chang then carved woodblocks to circulate [the text].

At the beginning of the Yuan Zhizheng era, the śramaṇa Juelin Juzong of Huangyan obtained a copy in Yizhen and returned to carve it at Yunfeng Zhengdao Monastery. Not long after, it was destroyed by fire. (From the *Xuexue*).
Cheng Gong once received the scriptures from Jue Lin and intended to carry on his predecessor’s legacy.

He therefore re-carved the woodblocks for publication, supplementing them with the explanations of names and categories provided by Chan Master Bai of Fuguo, which he appended after the "Guan" (Contemplations). This was done so that people might thoroughly understand their underlying meaning and intent.

Only the Venerable Sūtra of Prajñāpāramitā universally encompasses all phenomena of form and mind within both the mundane and supramundane realms, bringing them all back to the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Its efficacy is inconceivable. It is like the waters of the four great oceans, vast and boundless;

yet, were they gathered and drawn into a single pore, there would be no increase or decrease, and the original characteristics of those great oceans would remain as they were. That is to say, when expanded, it is...

The Great Encompassing has no exterior; when rolled up, it enters the smallness that has no interior. With the wisdom of skillful means, Xueyue (Snow Moon) created this method for penetrating the gateway.
In the space of a single finger-snap, he was able to master one-sixth of the entire scripture. His benefit to all sentient beings was immense.
The father and son of the Snow Mountains were also able to devote themselves to its propagation, fearing only that they might be too late. All of them—
One has fulfilled the entrustment of the former Buddhas. Nevertheless, within the nature of true awakening, not a single word is established;

it is luminous, supreme, and illuminates all without obstruction. All the texts compiled by Mahā-Ānanda and others that were entered into the Tripiṭaka manifested one by one from within this very radiance.
Those who encounter these gates, if they seek them here, will find that the mountains, rivers, and the great earth...
Whether animate or inanimate, all things together form the body of the text; there is no need to deliberate upon the relative complexity or brevity of its scrolls.
Xue Shan traveled extensively to consult masters in various regions and once served as the keeper of the treasury at Lingyin Jingde Chan Monastery.
His resolve to defend the Way was truly resplendent. Preface by Song Lian, Academician and Lecturer at the Hanlin Academy, Jinhua.
The First Section on the Essential Dharma of the Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra.
Disciple under the Bodhisattva Precepts, Zhujing,
pays homage with praise to the Mother of all Buddhas, the pure and supreme vehicle, the boat and bridge for crossing the ocean of suffering.
Darkly painted, he suspends the sun and moon; holding a firm and sharp vajra, he destroys the mountains of affliction with a lion’s roar.
He shatters the hearts of jackals; as the Lord of Śākya silently maintains meditative concentration, the demonic armies naturally fall away and dissolve.
With his jewel-palms, he holds mani-gems, which manifest in five colors according to the directions.
In the celestial palaces, food and vessels appear together; A hundred flavors arise according to the mind’s intent.

The number of verses exceeds a *saṃkhyeya*, and the wisdom-transcendence (*prajñāpāramitā*) surpasses all limits. Gathering these lofty and vast meanings, I have condensed them into the secret pivot in three fascicles.
Its unfolding exceeds half a division [of the canon], With its wondrously adorned verses revolving in cycles.
Whirling wheels of radiant light, A dense web of shadows arrayed in rows; The sounds of the walking trees intermingle.
Within this single atom, The Great Thousandfold Sūtras flow forth. In a single thought-moment, one can travel throughout immeasurable kalpas;
Awakening through cultivation, one ascends to the stage of enlightenment, Accumulating extraordinary merit through writing and recitation.
Hearing and listening arise from initial conditions; Slight slander brings forth the seeds of retribution.
From the Peak of Existence above Down to the Avīci Hell below, All stem from the divisions of deluded views.
Failing to reach the true place of refuge, One perceives the four marks as like illusions And knows that all phenomena are fundamentally empty; Thus may we board the vessel of Prajñā together.

First, look at the instructional notes on the characters; only then will one understand that there are additions and deletions within the fundamental dharma-positions.)

Revised and rearranged. Upon entering the Pass, the beginning, middle, and end were organized one by one in sequence, totaling approximately three hundred fascicles. These were divided into six sections (*cè*).

For the five subsequent sections, one must seek the praises (*zàn*) in the preceding fascicles; every character of these praises indicates the title and points toward the Dharma according to this standard.
Master Xuanzang’s eighty-fascicle version corresponds to this current collection; the fifth section is currently in circulation.
The Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra: Section on the Dharma, Scroll One.
Compiled by Shi Liang Chiyuetang Shi Yonglong.
Form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The sense bases (*āyatana*): the eye base, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind bases;
the form base, the sound, odor, taste, tangible object, and mental phenomena bases.
The elements (*dhātu*): the eye element, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind elements.
The realm of form, the realms of sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena;
the realm of eye-consciousness, and the realms of ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-consciousness;
and eye-contact, ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact.
The various feelings produced with eye-contact as condition; the various feelings produced with ear-, nose-, tongue-, body-, and mind-contact as conditions.
The earth element; the water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness elements.
The causal conditions: the immediately preceding condition, the object condition, and the dominant condition.

The phenomena produced by these conditions—namely, from ignorance and volitional formations, there arise consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, clinging, becoming, birth, and finally, old age.
Death brings grief, lamentation, suffering, sorrow, and despair.

[These are countered by] the perfection of generosity, the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of diligence, the perfection of meditative concentration, and the perfection of wisdom.
Emptiness of the internal; emptiness of the external; (then) emptiness of both the internal and external; emptiness of emptiness; great emptiness; emptiness of the ultimate truth;
emptiness of the conditioned; emptiness of the unconditioned; absolute emptiness; boundless emptiness; emptiness of dispersion; emptiness of non-alteration;
emptiness of intrinsic nature; emptiness of self-characteristics; emptiness of common characteristics; emptiness of all phenomena. Not...
The emptiness of obtainability; the emptiness of non-existence; the emptiness of intrinsic nature (up to) the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of non-existence;

suchness; the dharma-realm (which is) the dharma-nature, the non-falsehood, the non-alteration, the equality, the state beyond birth, the fixedness of dharmas, the stability of dharmas, the reality-limit, and the sphere of empty space (up to) the...
The inconceivable realm:
the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, and the seven factors of enlightenment.
(Up to) the eight factors of the noble path;
the noble truth of suffering, the noble truths of origin, cessation, and the path;
the four dhyānas; the four immeasurables; and the four formless attainments.
The eight liberations, the eight bases of mastery, the nine successive attainments, the ten totalities, and the gates of liberation:
emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
All dhāraṇī-doors; all samādhi-doors.

The Stage of Utmost Joy, the Stage Free from Defilement, (then) the Radiant Stage, the Stage of Blazing Wisdom, the Stage Difficult to Conquer, the Manifest Stage, the Far-Reaching Stage, the Immovable Stage, the Stage of Excellent Intelligence, (up to) the Cloud of Dharma Stage.
The five eyes, the six supernormal powers,
the ten powers of a Buddha, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha,
great loving-kindness, great compassion, great sympathetic joy, and great equanimity.
The thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty secondary characteristics;
the quality of non-forgetfulness and the constant abiding in equanimity;
omniscience, the knowledge of the paths, and the knowledge of all aspects.
The fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner, the non-returner, the fruit of arhatship,
the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha,
all the practices of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, and the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment of all buddhas.

Furthermore, Śāriputra, when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (entering the gateway),
they do not perceive form— or feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness— as either associated or dissociated.
(Next, regarding form: furthermore, from the other upper and lower realms, it arises from non-seeing. Form arises up to the Buddha’s bodhi and enters my sentient beings.
Within the fundamental dharma, one takes the dharmas produced by conditions; add the character "sheng" (生) above and the character "zhu" (諸) below.
It extends uniformly as far as ignorance. Afterwards, it enters the two sections of the desire realm, then enters from giving up to the fourth [dhyāna].)
The Truths (*satya*). Next, one enters the ten wholesome paths of action (*daśa-kuśala-karmapatha*) and the four stages (*catuḥ-pada*). Only then does the fundamental method enter the four dhyānas.

To the section on the realm of great compassion (*mahāmaitrī-dhātu*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) are added below. Then, regarding the eighteen Buddha-qualities (*aṣṭādaśa-buddhadharma*), "all-aspect omniscience" (*sarvākārajñatā*) is added below;
subsequently, one enters "omniscience" (*sarvajñajñāna*) along with the two sections on its permanent eradication [of afflictions]. Only then does one enter the four fruits up to Bodhi.
[The section on] Ignorance (*avidyā*) follows later and enters into my Seventeen Dharmas, divided into two sections for the upper and lower realms, before entering the main text:
the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*), the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*), and the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). (In the latter two sections, Ignorance follows later and enters.)
The ten paths of wholesome action; the five precepts of a lay follower (*upāsaka*); the eight precepts of the one-day fast (*upoṣadha*).
The meritorious activities consisting of generosity; those consisting of ethical discipline; and those consisting of cultivation (the four preceding sections are entered after the Four Noble Truths).

The knowledge of all modes of knowledge (*sarvajñajñāna*) forever uproots all habitual tendencies of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*). [This follows the two preceding sections on the subtle wisdom of all aspects.
I, sentient being, life-principle, creature, nourisher, person, *pudgala*, mind-born, youth, agent, instigator, originator, prompter, and experiencer.
[This causes] the recipient, the knower, and the seer [to realize it]. (The two preceding sections on Bodhi are followed here by the entry into the main discourse.

Śāriputra, by this cause and condition, you should know that when Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they are said to be in union with the perfection of wisdom. Furthermore, Śāriputra, all...
When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), they do not observe emptiness as being associated with or dissociated from emptiness;
they do not observe signlessness as being associated with or dissociated from signlessness;
they do not observe wishlessness as being associated with or dissociated from wishlessness. Why is this? Śāriputra, emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness are all non-existent.
"Because of being associated or dissociated, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
they are said to be 'associated with the perfection of wisdom' because they are associated with such dharmas.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom..."
Having entered into the emptiness of the intrinsic characteristics of all phenomena, one does not observe form as either associated or dissociated;
one does not observe feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either associated or dissociated.
This bodhisattva mahāsattva does not observe form as being associated or dissociated with the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). Why? Because he does not perceive a prior limit. He does not observe...
One does not observe whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are associated or dissociated with the prior limit (*pūrvānta*). Why? Because the prior limit is not perceived.
One does not observe whether form is associated or dissociated with the posterior limit (*aparānta*). Why? Because the posterior limit is not perceived.
One does not observe whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are associated or dissociated with the posterior limit. Why? Because the posterior limit is not perceived.
For this reason, because they do not perceive the future limit, they do not observe whether form is associated or dissociated with the present.
Why? Because they do not perceive the present. They do not observe whether feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness are associated or dissociated with the present.
Why? Because they do not perceive the present. Furthermore, Śāriputra, all bodhisattvas...
Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not contemplate whether the past limit and the future limit are associated or dissociated;
does not contemplate whether the past limit and the present are associated or dissociated;
does not contemplate whether the future limit and the past limit are associated or dissociated; nor does he contemplate the future limit and the present.
Whether associated or dissociated, one does not contemplate the present as being associated or dissociated with the past;

one does not contemplate the present as being associated or dissociated with the future; one does not contemplate the past, the future, or the present as being associated or dissociated with one another;
nor does one contemplate the future, the past, or the present [in such a manner].
Whether associated or dissociated, one does not contemplate the present as being associated or dissociated with the past or the future;
nor does one contemplate the past or the future as being associated or dissociated with the present. Why is this?
Śāriputra, it is because the three times are empty. Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom...
If a pāramitā is associated with such dharmas, it should be said to be associated with the prajñāpāramitā.
(Entering the primary gate; arising again in the upper realms; not observing arising in the lower realms.)
[The upper and lower realms are a single dharma; each is exhausted by the subsequent invocation of Śāriputra’s formulation).

perception, mental formations, and consciousness?
(The higher realms arise again in succession. The lower realms do not observe entry into the three periods of time. Having resolved the bonds above and below, one enters the five aggregates.
Reaching the realm of the Buddha’s Bodhi, the realms above and below invoke the subsequent bond of Śāriputra. Internally, the superior condition descends.)

The entry and the dharmas produced from conditions—excluding their original positions—are all situated in the lower realms. The Great Compassion Realm flows into the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).
Beyond ignorance, there are two types: the extensive and the concise. Below the ten powers of the Buddha, the realms include the concise;

internally, there is no *tathatā* (suchness) among the four fruits. There are five realms for the practices of the solitary realizers (*pratyekabuddha*), bodhisattvas, and those proceeding toward perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), extending to the first.
All-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñatā) directly enters the two segments of the subsequent Buddha’s bodhi;
having returned, it enters the mutual identity of the Buddha-wisdom aspect and the bodhi aspect—these two segments are completed (entry into the pass).
The past, the future, and the present—
the Buddha’s awakening.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),...
One does not contemplate whether all-knowledge is associated or dissociated with the Buddha;
nor does one contemplate whether awakening is associated or dissociated with the Buddha.
(Bodhi). Why is this?
All-knowledge is itself the Buddha; the Buddha is itself all-knowledge;
therefore it is bodhi. (Bodhi).

(The preceding text concludes the discussion on the Buddha’s Bodhi within the fundamental dharma. It enters into the mutual identity of the characteristics of the Buddha’s wisdom, reaching all-knowledge (*sarvajñā*).

Furthermore, it enters into the mutual identity of the characteristics of Bodhi, passing through two recitations to conclude the section. It then enters the "Gate of the Various Characters" [the root text]).
Śāriputra, because bodhisattva mahāsattvas who practice the perfection of wisdom are associated with such dharmas,
they should be said to be associated with the perfection of wisdom.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra, when bodhisattva-mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom,
they do not cling to form [and so forth, as detailed at length], nor do they cling to existence."
(Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness) &;

[The upper realms arise again; they arise without attachment to the lower realms. Once each upper and lower realm is understood, reaching the point where the first character of the "Manifest" [section] is invoked, Śāriputra concludes that because there is no attachment to the existence of form (*rūpa*), one speaks of the non-existence of form.

Next, he speaks of the existence and non-existence of the four aggregates (*skandha*), and then replaces "form is permanent" with "the four aggregates are impermanent," treating them as one and the same.]
Pleasure and suffering continue until the presence of aspiration; following this, the subsequent sections are categorized into sixteen gates, which together constitute eight dharmas.

Among these, one dharma is extensive while fifteen dharmas are abbreviated. Regarding the dharmas produced by internal conditions, they are included within the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

In the section on Pratyekabuddhas, they are added below the Arhats. As for the realm of great compassion, it is included within the unimpeded analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*); there are further expansions and abbreviations below, continuing up to Bodhi.

Part One: Chapter Seven, "Instruction and Admonition," Part One.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the Venerable Subhūti: "By means of your eloquence, you should [speak] for the sake of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

He proclaimed the Dharma associated with the *prajñāpāramitā* and instructed and exhorted the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to reach the ultimate consummation in the study and practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
At that time, the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as the great śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, all had this thought: "Now, the Honored One..."
"O Subhūti, by the power of your own wisdom and eloquence, you shall proclaim the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;

you shall instruct and admonish those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they may reach the ultimate consummation in the study of the perfection of wisdom. Will you do this by relying on the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power?"

[It is] so. Venerable Subhūti, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, as well as those of the great śrāvakas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, non-humans, and others, addressed the venerable Śāriputra, saying:
"You should know that all the teachings spoken by the disciples of the Buddhas are sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power. Why is this? Śāriputra, all..."

The Buddha proclaims the essential points of the Dharma for others. Having received the Buddha’s instruction, they practice and study with diligence, thereby able to realize the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*).
Consequently, whatever they proclaim for others will never be in contradiction with that true nature.
Therefore, the words of the Buddha are like a lamp that transmits its light. Śāriputra, I shall now, relying upon the majestic power and empowerment of the Buddha, [proceed] for the sake of all...
The assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas proclaimed the teachings associated with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā),
instructing and admonishing the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas so that they might reach the ultimate consummation in the study and practice of the perfection of wisdom.
This is not by the power of one's own wisdom or eloquence. Why is this?

Because the Dharma associated with the profound *prajñāpāramitā* is not within the sphere of experience of any *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*. At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, as the Buddha has commanded, you [should] by means of your eloquence proclaim [this] for the assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."

He teaches the Dharma associated with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), instructing and training the bodhisattva mahāsattvas so that they may reach the ultimate consummation in the study of the perfection of wisdom.
"Bhagavān, in this context, what dharma is called 'bodhisattva mahāsattva'? Furthermore, what dharma is called 'perfection of wisdom'? Thus he asked the Bhagavān.
I do not perceive any dharma that can be called a bodhisattva mahāsattva,
nor do I perceive any dharma that can be called the prajñāpāramitā. Since these two names themselves are not perceived to exist,
how can I proclaim for the assembly of bodhisattva mahāsattvas the dharmas associated with the prajñāpāramitā, or provide them with instruction and admonition?
[The Buddha] bestows [this teaching] upon the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, causing them to reach the ultimate consummation in the study and practice of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
The Buddha said, "Subhūti, the 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva' is merely a name; it is called a 'bodhisattva-mahāsattva' by way of a mere designation.
The *prajñāpāramitā* is also merely a name; it is called *prajñāpāramitā* by way of a mere designation. Thus, these two names..."
Moreover, Subhūti, these two names are merely names; they are neither born nor extinguished. They exist only as conceptualization, designation, and verbal expression.
Such conventional designations do not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between the two, because they are ungraspable.
“Buddha” (Subhūti, you should know): for example, “I” (is) merely a provisional (designation).
Furthermore, Subhūti, “form” (is a) phenomenon.
In this way, what is called a "self," a "dharma," "form," and so forth— likewise,

a "sentient being," a "life-principle," a "born one," a "nourisher," a "person," a "pudgala," a "mind-born," a "youth," an "agent," a "causer of action," an "ariser," a "causer of arising," an "experiencer," a "causer of experience," a "knower," or a "seer"— is likewise merely a conventional designation.
(Phenomena) &; ○ Thus &; (Names) &;
are conventional designations. They are neither born nor extinguished. There are only conceptualizations, designations, and verbal expressions, such as "sentient beings" up to "seers" &;
(abbreviated) &; (phenomena).

All such things exist merely as provisional designations. These provisional designations do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between the two, because they are unobtainable.
Thus, Subhūti, whether it be a bodhisattva mahāsattva, or the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), or these two names—all are provisional phenomena (*prajñapti-dharma*).

Thus, [as provisional phenomena], they are neither born nor extinguished; they exist only as conceptualizations, designations, and verbal expressions, referred to as "bodhisattva mahāsattva" or "perfection of wisdom."

The designation of "Dharma" and these two names—these three kinds exist merely as provisional designations (*prajñapti*). These various designations do not exist internally, nor do they exist externally, nor do they exist in between the two;
for they are ungraspable. [End of first scroll. In the main text, these characters are called out; the others are not. ... Conditioned by eye-contact, it finally enters...

From "the internal body" up to "illusory phenomena," and from "form" up to "illusory phenomena," all proceed from the letter *buddha*. Furthermore, they arise from the thought: "I should know that these arise from Subhūti.
From "the internal body" up to "illusory phenomena," there is one expansion and one contraction; yet, upon returning, it is called merely a provisional name.
Reaching the first circular mark, one directly leaps into the second circular mark. Thus, this is called the provisional; one departs from illusory phenomena.
[End. (Concluding the sutra by repeating the final phrase).
All things belonging to the internal body, such as the head and neck, shoulders, arms, abdomen, back, chest, ribs, waist, spine, thighs, knees, calves, shins, down to the feet;
and all things belonging to external objects, such as grasses, trees, roots, stems, branches, leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
All Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future,

△ First Division, Chapter Sixteen: Praise of the Mahāyāna, Part Six.

Ordinary beings, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, tathāgatas, and Subhūti—ordinary beings cannot be apprehended in the past, ordinary beings cannot be apprehended in the future, and ordinary beings cannot be apprehended in the present.
Ordinary beings are also not to be apprehended within the equality of the three times. Why is this so?
Subhūti, within equality, neither the past, the future, nor the present (ordinary beings) can be apprehended. Why is this?
Because within equality, even the nature of equality itself cannot be apprehended; how much less could there be a past, future, or present (ordinary being) to be apprehended within equality?
This is because [the categories] from "self" and "sentient being" up to "knower" and "seer" do not exist.
Because it can be attained.
(The preceding section resumes from Subhūti; the mention of "śrāvakas" below occurs only twice. Upon entering the main sūtra, the chapter title is changed.

Subhūti, when bodhisattva mahāsattvas practice the perfection of wisdom, they abide within this mark of the equality of the three times and diligently train in the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
Because they are free from grasping and attachment, they swiftly attain full completion.
Subhūti, this is called the mark of the Great Vehicle—the equality of the three times—of the bodhisattva mahāsattva. If a bodhisattva...

“Mahāsattva, by abiding thus within the characteristics of this Great Vehicle, one surpasses all the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, and is swiftly able to realize the knowledge of all modes (sarvajñajñāna) for the benefit and happiness of sentient beings.
At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, excellent, excellent! The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has well spoken and rightly explained.”
“Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, this is the Great Vehicle. World-Honored One, such is the Great Vehicle—most honored and most sublime.
The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, having trained in this, attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).

The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the future, by training in this, shall attain the knowledge of all modes. [The bodhisattva-mahāsattvas] of the present, throughout the ten directions, immeasurable and...”
Countless bodhisattva-mahāsattvas in infinite worlds have studied in this [Dharma], and now they have attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*).
For this reason, the Mahāyāna is most honored and most sublime; it is the true and supreme basis for the knowledge of all modes.
The Buddha said to Subhūti: "So it is, so it is! It is just as you have said. All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the past, future, and present..."
Bodhisattvas all rely upon the Mahāyāna to practice with diligent application, thereby swiftly realizing unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
For this reason, the Mahāyāna is most honored and most sublime.
△ Chapter Seventeen: Accordance, Part One.

At that time, Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the Tathāgata previously instructed the Venerable Subhūti to proclaim the *prajñāpāramitā* for the sake of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas;
why is it that he now speaks of the Great [Vehicle]?"

[The Buddha] said, "Vehicle. The Venerable Subhūti then addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, will what I have just spoken regarding the Great Vehicle not perhaps contravene the *prajñāpāramitā*?
The Buddha told Subhūti, "What you have just spoken regarding the Great Vehicle is entirely in accord with the *prajñāpāramitā*; it does not contravene it at all. Why is this? Subhūti, all..."

“Wholesome dharmas, factors conducive to enlightenment, whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all such things as these are without exception subsumed within the perfection of wisdom.
At that time, the venerable Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, what are all those wholesome dharmas, factors conducive to enlightenment, or [dharmas of] śrāvakas?”
“Are the dharmas of the śrāvakas, the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of the bodhisattvas, and the dharmas of the buddhas all entirely subsumed within the perfection of wisdom?
The Buddha said, “Subhūti, they are.”
"Darkness" refers to [the absence of] the perfection of generosity and the perfection of ethical discipline (if one contemplates the upper and lower realms continuously,
excluding the eight liberations internally, and completely superimposing the gate of liberation through emptiness, there is no loss of mindfulness).
[The Dharma]... (later included in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*).

Subhūti, all such wholesome dharmas as these—the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*), whether they be the dharmas of śrāvakas, the dharmas of pratyekabuddhas, the dharmas of bodhisattvas, or the dharmas of buddhas—all of these are entirely subsumed within the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Pāramitā. (Entering) "Smearing.
Furthermore, Subhūti, whether it be the Mahāyāna or the Prajñāpāramitā, [it is] extensive.
(dhyāna); (rūpa); (vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna).
The wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, the determinate and indeterminate dharmas, the outflowing and non-outflowing dharmas,
the conditioned and unconditioned dharmas, and the mundane and supramundane dharmas of the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm—
the Dharma and Vinaya realized and taught by all Tathāgatas and Buddhas.
(From the Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā, up to the end of Tathatā [Suchness]. For both the upper and lower realms, the character *ruo* [若] is used as the starting point.

Regarding the six internal consciousnesses, the lower realm lacks the character *ruo*. The six perfections proceed in reverse order; having added *boluo* [波羅] to *shibo* [施], one then enters the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Following ignorance (*avidyā*), one enters the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Having completed the seven worldly dharmas, one enters the four dhyānas, up to all the *dhāraṇīs*. )
The *dhāraṇī*. Entering the two dharmas of all Tathāgatas; entering the suchness (*tathatā*) of internal emptiness; subsequently entering the *saṃyukta-āgama*;
and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñatā*) situated below the unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*).
All such phenomena as these are neither associated nor dissociated; they are neither with form nor without form;
neither visible nor invisible; neither resistant nor non-resistant; they all share a single characteristic, namely, the characteristic of being without characteristics (*animitta*).
Subhūti, for this reason, that which you have just described as the Great Vehicle is entirely in accord with the Prajñāpāramitā and does not deviate from it in any way. Why is this so?
“Susthitamati,” said the Buddha, “the Great Vehicle is not different from the Prajñāpāramitā, and the Prajñāpāramitā—whether extensive or concise—is not different from the Great Vehicle. Why is this?
Whether it be the Great Vehicle or the Prajñāpāramitā, their nature is non-dual and cannot be divided into two.”

Therefore, [the path] arises from Prajñāpāramitā. The six perfections proceed in reverse order; two additional pāramitās are added. Even in the lower realms, they are called "Sudhana" (Good Manifestation), extending through to the "Dharma of Non-forgetfulness.
The three internal wisdoms are included under the "Unshared Dharmas" (Āveṇika-dharmas). The subsequent sections follow this same pattern. [Otherwise, there would be] an error.

Following the Dharma, one enters into the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth, which are both empty and non-empty. There is a section from a *saṃyukta-āgama* (Connected Discourse) that modifies this chapter;
from here it continues until the character "zhǔ" (杵). [The section on] inner emptiness and suchness follows after the samādhi, and one enters the Śrāvaka-yāna.

Subhūti, by this cause and condition, that which you have just described as the Great Vehicle is entirely in accordance with the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā) and does not deviate from it in any way.
To speak of the Great Vehicle is, in fact, to have already spoken of the perfection of wisdom.
Much. If one speaks of the *prajñāpāramitā*, then one has already spoken of the Mahāyāna; for these two dharmas are without distinction.

World-Honored One, throughout all phenomena, in every way, in all places, and at all times, I have sought a bodhisattva...
“O Mahāsattva, there is absolutely nothing to be seen; ultimately, it cannot be apprehended.
How then can I instruct and admonish the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas by means of the Prajñāpāramitā? World-Honored One, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva exists only as a provisional designation.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is non-existent and unapprehendable. Apart from form, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva is non-existent and unapprehendable. For what reason do you say:
"In all dharmas, in every way, in every place, and at every time, I have sought the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, yet I saw nothing at all and could not apprehend him"? Why?

For what reason is it said that, just as "I" and so forth are ultimately unarisen, all phenomena (*dharmas*) likewise lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)? For what reason...

For what reason is it said that if they are ultimately unarisen, they cannot be designated as "form" and so forth?

because [sentient beings] are vast and non-existent. Thus, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva cannot be apprehended in the past, future, or present limits,

Form, feeling, perception, mental formations,
and consciousness are not different from the bodhisattva mahāsattva,
whether in the past limit or the future limit.

[in the] past [limit], [in the] future [limit],

With banners, streamers, and canopies—wondrous, marvelous, and extraordinary—and with music, lamps, and all that exists, they offer worship, respect, reverence, and praise.

According to what is taught in this sutra, those sons and daughters of good family who, reflecting in accordance with reality, write down such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, bestow it upon others for them to uphold, and cause it to spread widely; this...
Of these two accumulations of merit, the latter is greater. Why is this? Because by giving to others, one enables immeasurable and boundless sentient beings to attain the joy of the Dharma.

One gradually realizes the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. A person belonging to the lineage of a bodhisattva likewise trains with diligent effort in this very profound perfection of wisdom, thereby transcending the stages of both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

For this reason, Kauśika, if good sons and good daughters wish to offer immeasurable, supreme, and exquisite flower garlands, powdered incense, scattered perfumes, and the like;
robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, and parasols; various wonderful and rare treasures; and musical instruments—
With lamps illuminating everything that exists, one should offer worship, reverence, respect, and praise to the present Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas.
One should likewise write down this profound Prajñāpāramitā and honor it with immeasurable varieties of exquisite flower garlands,
powdered incense, scattered perfumes, garments, necklaces, precious banners, flags, parasols, various wonderful rarities, and musical instruments.
Lamp-lighters, exhausting all that they possess, made offerings, paid homage, revered, and praised him.
Kauśika, when I contemplated this matter, upon first attaining unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, I reflected: "Upon whom shall I rely for my dwelling?
Who is capable of receiving my offerings, homage, reverence, and praise? While I was reflecting thus, I did not perceive anyone at all in the entire world...
"Whether they be devas, māras, brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, humans, non-humans, or anyone else, there is none who is my equal, much less any who could surpass me.
Furthermore, he reflected to himself: "Relying upon this Dharma, I have already realized unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
This Dharma is subtle, profound, and tranquil; I shall abide by relying upon this very Dharma and make offerings to it."
Reverence, honor, and praise. What is this dharma? It is the Prajñāpāramitā.
Kauśika, even though I have already attained Buddhahood, I still follow this profound Prajñāpāramitā, abiding in accordance with it, making offerings, revering, honoring, and praising it;
how much more so for good sons and good daughters who wish to seek [the unsurpassed path]?
Having set their minds upon unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, they do not take this profound *prajñāpāramitā* as their heartfelt refuge nor diligently train in it;
yet, with immeasurable varieties of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incense perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, and canopies,
along with various wonderful rarities, music, and lamps— offering all that they possess, they pay homage and provide offerings.

One should revere, respect, and praise it. Kauśika, if sons or daughters of good family seek the vehicle of the śrāvakas or the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, they too should take refuge with a sincere mind in this profound perfection of wisdom.

They shall diligently practice and study, making offerings, showing reverence, honoring, respecting, and praising [this] with immeasurable kinds of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and incensed perfumes, robes, necklaces, precious banners, flags, and canopies, as well as all manner of rare treasures, wondrous curiosities, music, and lamps—giving up everything they possess.
Why is this, Kauśika? Because such a Prajñāpāramitā is able to give birth to...
From this assembly of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas arise;
and based upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are born.
For this reason, Kauśika, any sons of good family who seek the Mahāyāna, the Pratyekabuddhayāna, or the Śrāvakayāna—
Virtuous women and others should all take refuge with a sincere heart in this profound Prajñāpāramitā and diligently practice and study it,
offering immeasurable varieties of exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes, and necklaces.
With jeweled banners, canopies, and all manner of exquisite rarities, as well as music, lamps, and light—offering everything they possess—they worship, revere, honor, and praise [this].

Why is this? Because those who seek the state of a Śrāvaka, by diligently practicing and studying this Prajñāpāramitā, ultimately realize the fruit of Arhatship; and those who seek the state of a Pratyekabuddha, through this Prajñā...
By diligently training in the perfections (pāramitās), one ultimately realizes the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. Those who seek the Great Vehicle (mahāyāna) will,
by diligently training in this perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā), ultimately realize unexcelled, perfect,
and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi).

Place it on Jambudvīpa; place it on Pūrvavideha Island; place it on Aparagodānīya Island;

Manifesting transformations throughout the trichiliocosm;
manifesting transformations throughout worlds in the ten directions each as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
manifesting transformations throughout all worlds in the ten directions.

"Suppose they were all made to practice and study the ten paths of wholesome action, as well as the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers.
What do you think, Śakra, Lord of the Devas? Would those sons and daughters of good family obtain much merit by reason of this?"
[He] said: "Very much, World-Honored One; very much, Sugata. The Buddha said:

"Kauśika, if sons or daughters of good family were to write down this profound *prajñāpāramitā*, give it to others for reading and recitation, or transcribe it themselves and cause it to be widely circulated, the mass of merit obtained by those sons and daughters of good family would be very great."
As stated previously. Why is this? Kauśika, within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, all untainted (anāsrava) dharmas are extensively expounded.
Persons belonging to the lineage of the śrāvakas train in these dharmas.

They swiftly enter the noble state of certainty (*samyaktva-niyāma*) and attain the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), the fruit of once-returning (*sakṛdāgāmi-phala*), the fruit of non-returning (*anāgāmi-phala*), and the fruit of arhatship (*arhat-phala*).

A person (*pudgala*) of the pratyekabuddha lineage who trains in this Dharma swiftly enters the noble state of certainty of a pratyekabuddha and gradually realizes the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha. A person of the bodhisattva lineage...

Rāhula, by training in this Dharma, one swiftly enters the bodhisattva’s state of rightness beyond birth (*samyaktva-niyāma*), gradually practices all the bodhisattva deeds, and realizes unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Kausika, within this secret treasury of the Prajñāpāramitā, all untainted dharmas (*anāsrava-dharma*) are taught; that is to say, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*).
The six perfections are all extensive. When mindfulness reaches the gateways of all *samādhis*, one enters them, as well as the other textual passages.

Above the four *dhyānas*, the two characters "untainted" (*anāsrava*) are added. At the beginning of the four truths, the character "knowledge" (*jñāna*) is added; the remaining [realms] lack the dharmas of the four truths.

The gateway of liberation through the signless (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) is not related to the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*) exists only in the three continents.
...and other immeasurable and boundless Buddha-dharmas; all these are the untainted (anāsrava) dharmas explained herein.
Kauśika, if a son or daughter of good family were to instruct a single sentient being to abide in the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-phala*), [the merit thereof would be...]

The accumulation of merit thus obtained would still be superior to that of teaching and transforming all sentient beings throughout Jambudvīpa, causing them all to practice and study the ten paths of wholesome action,
as well as those in Jambudvīpa and Pūrvavideha.
Jambudvīpa; Pūrvavideha; Aparagodānīya; Jambudvīpa; Pūrvavideha;

(The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five supernormal powers);
the intermediate chiliocosm; likewise, the trichiliocosm.
"In each of the ten directions, there are worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
likewise, in all worlds throughout the ten directions.
Why is this so, Kauśika? Because those who practice [the ten paths of wholesome action] are not exempt from the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts."
(The four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, and the five superknowledges.
If sentient beings abide in the fruit of stream-entry, they immediately obtain permanent liberation from the three evil destinies;
how much more so for the mass of merit obtained by teaching them to abide in the fruits of once-returner, non-returner, or arhatship? And...

Kauśika, it is not as meritorious for a son or daughter of good family to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and establish them in the fruits of Stream-enterer, Once-returner, Non-returner, and Arhatship, as it would be for someone to instruct a single sentient being and cause them to dwell securely in Pratyekabuddha-enlightenment. Why is this, Kauśika? Because...
The merits possessed by one who has awakened to bodhi exceed those of the stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and others by hundreds of thousands of times. Kausika,
if a son or daughter of good family were to instruct all sentient beings in Jambudvīpa and cause them all to abide in the awakening of a solitary buddha (*pratyekabuddhabodhi*),
the mass of merit they would obtain would not equal that of a person who instructs a single sentient being to aspire toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete awakening (*anuttarasamyaksambodhi*).

"Bodhi. Why is this? Kausika, if one instructs sentient beings to incline toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment, one ensures that the Buddha-eye in the world will not be severed. Why is this so? It is because of the existence of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas."
There are then the fruits of stream-entry, once-returning, non-returning, and arhatship, as well as the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha.
It is because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas that there are Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas who realize unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Because there are bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, there exist the Buddha-jewel, the Dharma-jewel, and the Saṃgha-jewel,
to which all the world takes refuge and offers worship. For this reason, Kauśika, all the world—
including gods, Māras, Brahmās, śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, as well as asuras, humans, and non-humans— should, with immeasurable [reverence]...
With exquisite flower garlands, powdered and scattered incenses, robes and necklaces, jeweled banners, pennants, and parasols, and all manner of rare and wonderful things,
music, and lamps— offering all that they possess, they honor, revere, respect, and praise the bodhisattva mahāsattvas.

Kauśika, by this you should know that if a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to write down such profound *prajñāpāramitā*, bestow it upon others for them to read and recite, or transcribe it further so as to cause it to circulate widely, the mass of merit they obtain would be immeasurable and boundless, surpassing the previous mass of merit. Why is this? Because such *prajñāpāramitā*...
Because within the many secret treasuries, all the supreme and virtuous dharmas of both the mundane and supramundane realms are extensively expounded;
it is for this reason that the teachings are set forth within this secret treasury of the *prajñāpāramitā*.
(These eight lines all arise from this Prajñāpāramitā).

Furthermore, Subhūti, because the perfection of wisdom is pure, form is pure; [and so on for the other aggregates] because form is pure, the knowledge of all modes is pure.
Why is this? If the perfection of wisdom is pure, if form is pure, and if the knowledge of all modes is pure, these are not two, nor are they divided; there is no distinction between them.
Because there is no severance.

(Next, from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, up to the Buddha’s bodhi; changing "meditative absorption" [dhyāna] to "impulse" [saṃskāra] until reaching bodhi, totaling eighty-four headings.

Manifestation. Those in the lower realms do not address him as "Subhūti. There are two versions: the extensive and the abbreviated. Even when encountering the abbreviated version, the messenger avoids his original position and does not call out.
Whenever one reaches a point of completion, it signifies the end of the Buddha’s Bodhi.
"Furthermore, Subhūti, because the knowledge of all modes (*sarvajñajñāna*) is pure, form (*rūpa*) is pure;
because form is pure, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is pure. Why is this? If the knowledge of all modes is pure..."
Form is [omitted] pure. If the perfection of wisdom is pure, there is no duality and no division; they are not distinct and not separate.

[At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra] addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, such purity is most profound.
(Then Śāriputra again...)
The Buddha said, “It is so. Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked, “Because of the ultimate purity of what dharma is this purity said to be most profound?
The Buddha said, “Śāriputra, because form (*rūpa*) is ultimately pure, this purity is said to be most profound.”
(At the time when the most profound [wisdom] arises, it is extremely clear until reaching the state of non-arising and non-manifestation;

It is extremely lucid, non-reverting, and non-continuous; fundamentally free from defilement, its intrinsic nature is luminously pure, without attainment or observation, without arising or manifestation. [Yu]
(Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, [is it that] such purity is non-arising (in the desire realm)?
Śāriputra said this. The Buddha said, "It is so.
Because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra said, "In what way is such purity non-arising?"
(The realm of desire). The Buddha said: "Because the intrinsic nature of the realm of desire cannot be apprehended, one who is thus purified does not arise in the realm of desire.

[The teaching] is concluded. Upon entering the gates and traversing the upper and lower realms, [the Buddha] calls for Śāriputra each time, saying: "Form arises... until the end of Bodhi.
Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is such pure intrinsic nature devoid of cognition? The Buddha said:
"It is so, because it is ultimately pure. Śāriputra asked, "In what way is this pure intrinsic nature devoid of cognition?
The Buddha said, "Because the intrinsic nature of all phenomena is insentient, their pure intrinsic nature is devoid of cognition.

Therefore, Śāriputra asked: "In what way is the nature of form (and so forth, as abbreviated) being without cognition itself purity? The Buddha said:
"Because its intrinsic nature is empty, the nature of form (and so forth, as abbreviated) being without cognition is itself purity."
Then Śāriputra again addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, the *prajñāpāramitā* neither benefits nor harms omniscience (*sarvajñajñāna*).

"Because the realms (*dhātu*) are eternally constant, the *prajñāpāramitā* neither benefits nor harms omniscience (*sarvajñājñāna*).

At that time, the Venerable Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying, “World-Honored One, because I am pure, form is pure. The Buddha said, “So it is; because it is ultimately pure.”

At that time, Subhūti again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva can awaken to and know in this way, is this the prajñāpāramitā of a bodhisattva mahāsattva? The Buddha said: “It is so, because it is ultimately pure. Subhūti asked:
